title: Beat Inflation
learningObjective: Apply inflation, saving, budgeting, interest, and asset-versus-liability concepts to protect purchasing power as prices rise.
primaryMisconception: Keeping the same amount of money guarantees that a person will be able to afford the same things in the future.
secondaryMisconceptions: Cash always protects money from financial risk.
Any item that may help someone earn money is automatically a good asset.
A higher savings balance always means purchasing power has increased.
keyTakeaway: Money must grow or plans must adjust when prices rise faster than savings.

conceptsAssessed.concept: Access and storage through bank accounts.
Savings may earn interest without guaranteeing purchasing-power protection.
Growth can build over time while investment outcomes remain uncertain.
Debt depends on purpose, affordability, and repayment pressure.
Value depends on actual use, cost, and affordability.

overview.summary: Manage Rs. 100,000 across one year as a laptop rises from Rs. 100,000 to Rs. 115,000. Choose where to keep money, rebuild a monthly budget after prices rise, and judge asset and debt choices. Earlier decisions change access, goal progress, debt, and the final dashboard. The score rewards realistic decisions rather than luck.

startingState.financialGoal: Protect enough purchasing power for the laptop while keeping the monthly budget stable and avoiding unnecessary debt.

screens.title: Same Savings, Higher Price
screens.content: Your Rs. 100,000 once bought the laptop you wanted. One year later, it costs Rs. 115,000. Can your plan catch up?
screens.illustration: A laptop price changes from Rs. 100,000 to Rs. 115,000 while savings remain Rs. 100,000.

screens.title: Your Starting Position
screens.content: You begin with Rs. 100,000 in savings, Rs. 40,000 monthly income, no debt, and no investments.
screens.illustration: A dashboard showing savings, income, debt, and the laptop goal.

screens.title: The Number Did Not Shrink
screens.content: Your balance still says Rs. 100,000. The challenge is whether that amount can still buy what it could before.
screens.illustration: The same balance appears beside a higher laptop price.

screens.title: Three Decisions Remain
screens.content: Choose where to keep money, rebuild the monthly budget, and judge which purchases create value or pressure.
screens.illustration: Three decision cards show storage, budgeting, and asset choices.

screens.title: What Is the Main Risk?
screens.question: What is the biggest risk when savings stay the same but prices rise?

options.label: The bank removes the money
options.feedback: The scenario does not show money being removed.

options.label: The money buys less than before
options.feedback: Correct. The number is unchanged, but purchasing power is lower.

options.label: Every investment becomes safe
options.feedback: Rising prices do not remove investment risk.

options.label: Debt automatically becomes useful
options.feedback: Debt still depends on purpose and affordability.

screens.connectionToSimulation: The mission tests how storage, budgeting, and spending choices respond to reduced purchasing power.

stages.title: Purchasing Power
stages.timelineLabel: Start of Year vs One Year Later
stages.situation: One year ago, Rs. 100,000 bought one laptop. Today, savings are still Rs. 100,000, but the laptop costs Rs. 115,000.
stages.objective: Identify whether purchasing power increased, decreased, or stayed the same.

config.learnerQuestion: Has the purchasing power of Rs. 100,000 increased, decreased, or remained the same?
config.importantHiddenDifference: The balance is unchanged, but the goal price increased.
config.explanation: Rs. 100,000 now covers about 87% of the laptop. Purchasing power decreased.

choices.label: Increased
choices.immediateFeedback: The laptop became more expensive while savings did not rise.
choices.laterConsequence: The plan may not adjust for inflation.

choices.label: Decreased
choices.immediateFeedback: Correct. The same money no longer buys the same laptop.
choices.laterConsequence: Storage and saving decisions can address the real goal.

choices.label: Stayed the same
choices.immediateFeedback: The number stayed the same, but what it can buy changed.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Balance is confused with purchasing power.
choices.laterConsequence: The learner may fail to adapt.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Compare what money can buy, not only the account number.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: A stable number may still lose purchasing power.

validation.method: Require one answer and reveal the comparison.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Compare the higher laptop price with unchanged savings.
validation.retryBehaviour: Allow one retry after showing the affordability ratio.

accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Compare both rows and choose increased, decreased, or unchanged.

stateSummary.title: Purchasing Power Changed
stateSummary.learningMessage: The number can stay the same while purchasing power falls.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Choose where the Rs. 100,000 should have been kept.

stages.title: Choose Where to Keep Money
stages.situation: Rewind to the start of the year. The laptop may be needed within twelve months. Choose how to store Rs. 100,000 while balancing access, growth, and uncertainty.
stages.objective: Choose a storage approach that fits the goal date and ability to accept losses.

startingNode.question: Where should the Rs. 100,000 be kept?

educationalAssumptions: All rates and outcomes are fictional classroom assumptions.
The savings-account path uses 5% illustrative growth for one year.
The mixed path places Rs. 60,000 in savings and Rs. 40,000 in a basic investment.
The displayed investment change is +8%, but a real investment could rise or fall.
Decision quality is scored separately from the displayed result.

choices.label: Keep everything as cash
choices.immediateFeedback: The amount stays accessible but earns no growth in this simulation.
choices.laterConsequence: The laptop gap remains Rs. 15,000 before new contributions.

choices.label: Use a savings account
choices.immediateFeedback: The money remains accessible and earns Rs. 5,000 of illustrative growth.
choices.laterConsequence: The gap becomes Rs. 10,000 before new contributions.

choices.label: Spend everything immediately
choices.immediateFeedback: The money is no longer available for the laptop or unexpected needs.
choices.laterConsequence: The full Rs. 115,000 target must be rebuilt or borrowed.

choices.label: Split Rs. 60,000 into savings and Rs. 40,000 into a basic investment
choices.immediateFeedback: Some money stays accessible while another part accepts investment uncertainty.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The displayed path ends with Rs. 63,000 in savings and Rs. 43,200 invested.
choices.laterConsequence: The total reaches Rs. 106,200, but the invested part may not suit a near-term goal.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: For a goal likely needed within twelve months, a savings account is generally strong because access and lower uncertainty matter.
reasonableAlternatives: Cash may suit very short-term access while accepting weaker growth.
A mixed approach may suit money not needed soon when losses are acceptable.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More growth potential usually means more uncertainty or less immediate access.

validation.method: Accept one path and apply its balance changes.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: No path is universally invalid; review the time horizon and access needs.
validation.retryBehaviour: Allow review of every trade-off before confirmation.

accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose a storage approach and hear the access, growth, and risk effects.

stateSummary.title: Storage Strategy Applied

changedValues.reason: The savings paths earn classroom growth.
The mixed path includes an uncertain result.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Storage should fit the goal date, access needs, and risk tolerance.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Rising monthly costs now force the budget to change.

stages.title: Update the Budget
stages.situation: Food, transport, and mobile data now cost more. Monthly income remains Rs. 40,000. Rebuild the budget without pretending the old prices still apply.
stages.objective: Cover new essential costs, continue some saving, avoid debt where possible, and keep optional spending realistic.

choices.label: Cover new costs, continue saving, and keep affordable enjoyment
choices.immediateFeedback: The budget reflects current prices and protects present and future priorities.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Essential costs remain covered without new debt.
choices.laterConsequence: Annual savings help close the laptop gap.

choices.label: Remove all entertainment
choices.immediateFeedback: The maths may work, but the plan could become unnecessarily restrictive.
choices.laterConsequence: The plan may be harder to maintain.

choices.label: Stop saving completely
choices.immediateFeedback: Current costs are covered, but future goal progress stops.
choices.laterConsequence: The laptop gap depends only on the Stage 2 balance.

choices.label: Keep the old essential amounts
choices.immediateFeedback: The budget appears balanced only because it ignores the new prices.
choices.laterConsequence: Debt or missed needs may appear.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Update essential costs first, then adjust optional spending and saving without removing either automatically.
reasonableAlternatives: No entertainment may be reasonable for a short period.
A smaller saving amount may be reasonable when essential costs genuinely rise.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More saving closes the goal gap faster, while some enjoyment may make the plan sustainable.

validation.method: Check all essential minimums, total allocations at or below Rs. 40,000, and non-negative values.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Use the new prices and keep the total within Rs. 40,000.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep valid categories and highlight only the uncovered or overspent amount.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use labelled plus and minus buttons.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Adjust each category and hear the remaining balance and projected annual saving.

stateSummary.title: Budget Updated

changedValues.reason: Higher costs change the affordable amount.
The monthly plan determines yearly goal progress.
Stability depends on real costs, saving, and affordability.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Inflation may require the budget to change even when income does not.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Use the updated state to judge assets, costs, and debt.

stages.title: Asset or Cost?
stages.situation: Your storage choice and monthly saving plan have created a projected goal fund. Classify four financial choices, then decide how to handle the Rs. 115,000 laptop goal.
stages.objective: Judge value by actual use and affordability, then choose a goal action that fits the current state.

sortableItems.label: Laptop used for paid work
sortableItems.explanation: It may support income, but price, maintenance, and actual use still matter.

sortableItems.label: Luxury phone purchased with debt
sortableItems.explanation: It creates repayments and may lose value without producing income.

sortableItems.label: Course that improves work skills
sortableItems.explanation: Quality, suitability, and affordability must be checked; results are not guaranteed.

sortableItems.label: Unused subscription
sortableItems.explanation: It creates repeated cost without meaningful use.

config.ambiguityExplanation: An item is not automatically an asset because it might help someone earn. Actual use, quality, cost, and affordability matter.

finalDecision.question: What should you do about the Rs. 115,000 laptop goal?

choices.label: Buy the laptop when the goal fund covers it and the work use is clear
choices.immediateFeedback: The purchase is linked to a funded goal and a specific work purpose.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Rs. 115,000 is deducted from the goal fund.
choices.laterConsequence: The remaining balance stays available and no new debt is created.

choices.label: Cancel the unused subscription and continue saving
choices.immediateFeedback: A repeated unnecessary cost is removed and future saving improves.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Avoidable expenses fall by Rs. 1,500 monthly.
choices.laterConsequence: The laptop gap closes without new debt, but the purchase happens later.

choices.label: Borrow only the remaining laptop gap with a clear repayment plan
choices.immediateFeedback: The debt supports a work tool, but repayments must fit the budget.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Borrow up to Rs. 15,000 using six equal, interest-free classroom payments.
choices.laterConsequence: Budget stability falls if the repayment does not fit beside essentials and saving.

choices.label: Buy a luxury phone with Rs. 100,000 of debt
choices.immediateFeedback: The purchase creates a large obligation without supporting the laptop goal.
choices.laterConsequence: Budget stability and purchasing-power protection weaken.

choices.label: Spend Rs. 30,000 on a course without checking quality or affordability
choices.immediateFeedback: A course may create value, but this decision lacks evidence and affordability checks.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The goal fund falls by Rs. 30,000.
choices.laterConsequence: The laptop may be delayed and the course benefit remains uncertain.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Buy the laptop when it is funded, genuinely supports paid work, and does not destabilise the budget.
reasonableAlternatives: Continue saving after cancelling an unnecessary expense when the goal is underfunded.
Borrowing only a small gap may be reasonable when the laptop supports credible income and repayments fit.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Buying sooner may support work, while waiting or borrowing changes timing, access, and monthly pressure.

validation.method: Score all classifications, calculate the goal fund, and validate the final action.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: That action does not fit the current goal fund or repayment capacity.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep correct classifications and allow a different final action when affordability fails.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use three category buttons per item, then labelled final-action choices.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Classify each item and hear the current goal fund before choosing an action.

stateSummary.title: Purchasing-Power Plan Completed

changedValues.reason: The purchase, saving, or debt choice changes the laptop plan.
Unused or unverified purchases weaken the position.

stateSummary.learningMessage: An asset depends on use, affordability, and the pressure it creates.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Review how well the year protected purchasing power.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: The learner evaluates storage using the real Rs. 15,000 gap.
The cash path needs more saving to reach the laptop price.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows that access does not automatically protect purchasing power.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: Part of the goal fund depends on an uncertain investment value.
Regular saving may close the gap without debt.
Stopping savings leaves the goal dependent on the Stage 2 balance.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Shows the cost of ending goal progress.

consequenceMap.laterConsequence: The dashboard shows high debt and weaker stability.
consequenceMap.educationalPurpose: Connects optional debt with future pressure.

midMissionCheckpoint.title: Halfway Through the Year

positiveDecisionFeedbackRules.message: You recognised that the unchanged balance had lost purchasing power.
You kept a meaningful amount accessible for the near-term goal.

emergingRiskFeedbackRules.message: The balance has no growth in this classroom path while prices are higher.
A large part of the goal money is not immediately accessible.
The laptop goal must now be rebuilt from monthly income.

midMissionCheckpoint.reflectionQuestion: Continue to the inflation-adjusted budget, or review the storage choice first?

finalChallenge.title: Fund the Useful Goal
finalChallenge.situation: The laptop costs Rs. 115,000. Combine the current goal fund, monthly budget, asset judgement, and debt affordability before acting.
finalChallenge.recommendedReasoning: An item should create useful value, fit the budget, and avoid unnecessary debt pressure. Buying, waiting, or borrowing a small gap may each be reasonable depending on the current state.

debrief.title: Protect What Your Money Can Buy
debrief.content: You saw that an unchanged balance can lose purchasing power when prices rise. Storage choices changed access, growth, and uncertainty. The updated budget determined whether new saving could close the laptop gap. Finally, you judged whether a purchase could create useful value or mainly add cost and debt. Cash may suit short-term needs, while interest or investing may offer growth without guaranteeing that prices will be beaten. The strongest plan depends on the goal date, affordability, access needs, and risk tolerance—not the highest-risk choice.
debrief.simpleSummary: Protect purchasing power through realistic saving, budgeting, access, and careful spending.
debrief.illustration: A savings balance, budget, laptop goal, and debt meter connect around a rising-price arrow.

dimensions.label: Purchasing-Power Awareness
positiveRules: 15 for recognising decreased purchasing power.
5 for choosing unchanged and correcting the reasoning.
0 for choosing increased.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether you compared what money can buy, not only the account number.

dimensions.label: Storage and Access
positiveRules: 20 for the savings-account path for the near-term goal.
18 for a mixed path when the invested part is not needed soon.
12 for cash with clear short-term access reasoning.
2 for spending everything.
deductions: Mixed allocation falls to 10 when all money is needed within twelve months.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures how well access, possible growth, and uncertainty fit the goal.

dimensions.label: Budget Adjustment
positiveRules: 25 for covering new costs, continuing saving, and keeping enjoyment affordable.
22 for a valid no-entertainment plan.
12 for covering costs but stopping saving.
Invalid budgets must be revised.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether the budget reflects current prices and protects future goals.

dimensions.label: Asset and Debt Judgement
positiveRules: Up to 10 for correct classifications.
10 for a funded useful purchase.
9 for cancelling an unnecessary expense and continuing to save.
7 for a small affordable goal-gap loan.
0 for the luxury phone debt.
deductions: Deduct 4 for buying an unverified course without checking affordability.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether value, use, cost, and repayment pressure were considered together.

dimensions.label: Financial Adaptability
positiveRules: 20 when the goal is funded or on track, essentials remain covered, and avoidable debt is not created.
15 for a realistic delayed plan.
10 for a small affordable debt gap supporting a verified work tool.
0 when essentials are uncovered or optional debt creates major pressure.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures how well the plan changed when prices and costs changed.

performanceLevels.label: Purchasing Power At Risk
performanceLevels.description: The plan ignored rising prices, uncovered important costs, or created avoidable debt pressure.

performanceLevels.label: Building Protection
performanceLevels.description: Some choices protected access or saving, but the budget or goal plan still needs work.

performanceLevels.label: Financially Prepared
performanceLevels.description: The learner adjusted to higher prices while balancing access, saving, and affordability.

performanceLevels.label: Strong Inflation Response
performanceLevels.description: The learner made consistent, informed, and adaptable decisions. This does not guarantee future wealth.

resultsDashboard.explanationTemplate: Shows how much of the Rs. 115,000 laptop the final goal fund can cover.

resultsDashboard.label: Savings Growth
resultsDashboard.explanationTemplate: Separates new contributions from illustrative savings growth.

resultsDashboard.label: Basic Investment
resultsDashboard.explanationTemplate: Displays contributions separately from the fictional investment change.

resultsDashboard.label: Monthly Budget Stability
resultsDashboard.explanationTemplate: Measures whether the updated budget covers real costs, saving, and affordable enjoyment.

strengthRules.message: You recognised that the unchanged balance had lost purchasing power.
You rebuilt the budget around current prices without abandoning every future priority.
You judged value using actual use, affordability, and debt pressure.
Your adjusted plan restored enough purchasing power for the laptop goal.

improvementRules.message: Cash stayed accessible, but the goal still needed stronger saving or growth.
Stopping all saving protected today’s budget but weakened the future goal.
The debt choice created more pressure than lasting value.
Check actual use, quality, and affordability before calling a purchase an asset.

tradeoffRules.message: You prioritised access and lower uncertainty, accepting limited growth.
You accepted investment uncertainty for more growth potential.
You protected saving strongly, but the budget may be harder to maintain.
Borrowing accelerated a useful purchase but added a monthly repayment.

personalisedFeedbackRules.practicalPrinciple: Compare what money can buy, then adjust saving, spending, access, and risk around the real goal.
personalisedFeedbackRules.replayMessage: Replay with another storage or budget strategy to see how the laptop gap and debt options change.

questions.question: Which plan combines inflation awareness and budget adjustment most effectively?

options.label: Keep the old budget because income is unchanged
options.feedback: The old budget may not cover actual essential costs.

options.label: Update costs, continue some saving, and review optional spending
options.feedback: Correct. The plan responds to higher prices while protecting future progress.

options.label: Stop every enjoyable expense permanently
options.feedback: A realistic plan may include affordable enjoyment.

options.label: Borrow for every price increase
options.feedback: Debt does not remove the need to adjust the budget.

questions.correctExplanation: The plan uses current prices, maintains saving, and adjusts flexible spending.
questions.misconceptionTested: The same budget remains realistic when essential prices rise.

questions.question: Your savings balance is higher than last year. What must be checked before saying purchasing power improved?

options.label: Only the new account number
options.feedback: A larger number may still buy less if prices rose faster.

options.label: Whether the balance grew faster than the relevant prices
options.feedback: Correct. Purchasing power depends on both money and prices.

options.label: Whether all money was invested
options.feedback: Investing is not required and does not guarantee protection.

options.label: Whether every want was removed
options.feedback: Enjoyment spending is not the measure of purchasing power.

questions.correctExplanation: A higher balance protects purchasing power only when it keeps pace with relevant prices.
questions.misconceptionTested: A higher savings balance always means purchasing power increased.

questions.question: A Rs. 60,000 course may improve work skills, but paying for it would stop rent payments. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.label: It is automatically a good asset
options.feedback: Possible value does not remove affordability concerns.

options.label: Education is always profitable
options.feedback: Course quality and financial results are not guaranteed.

options.label: Its value depends on quality, use, affordability, and the missed rent
options.feedback: Correct. Potential value can still be unaffordable now.

options.label: Borrowing always makes it affordable
options.feedback: Borrowing adds repayment pressure and does not guarantee value.

questions.correctExplanation: Asset value depends on actual use and benefits as well as cost and affordability.
questions.misconceptionTested: Anything that may improve income is automatically a good asset.

completion.headline: Inflation Plan Complete!
completion.achievementMessage: You adjusted saving, budgeting, access, and spending decisions as prices changed.
completion.progressMessage: Journey Boss complete in Make Money Grow.
completion.nextTeaser: Next, explore how borrowing costs and repayment choices affect long-term flexibility.
completion.animation: A rising price arrow is matched by a stronger savings plan, stable budget, and completed laptop goal.

realLifeChallenge.title: Compare One Price
realLifeChallenge.instruction: Choose one fictional item, write last year’s price and a higher current price, then calculate the extra amount needed. Do not buy anything or share private financial information.

reviewChecklist.notes: Uses J2-M8 through J2-M13.

reviewChecklist.item: Does not introduce unexplained major concepts
reviewChecklist.notes: All terms appear through decisions and feedback.
Inflation, saving, budgeting, assets, and debt affect one goal.
Laptop, savings, and monthly budget calculations reconcile.
Balances, contributions, debt, and goal progress carry forward.
Storage and monthly saving change the final options.
Every major decision changes state, score, or later choices.

reviewChecklist.item: Multiple reasonable paths are allowed where appropriate
reviewChecklist.notes: Cash, savings, mixed allocation, waiting, and small goal debt may be defensible.
Purchasing power, interest, risk, affordability, and debt are represented accurately.
Uses salary, bills, saving goals, work tools, and debt.
Uses simple percentages and visible amounts.
All products and results are fictional classroom examples.
Investment outcomes are explicitly uncertain.
No real stock or market price is used.

reviewChecklist.item: No claims that markets always recover
reviewChecklist.notes: No recovery claim is made.

reviewChecklist.item: Simulated results are not presented as forecasts
reviewChecklist.notes: Rates and outcomes are labelled fictional.
Risky choices receive calm feedback.
Every strategy includes trade-offs.
Uses PKR, income, transport, mobile data, and a laptop goal.
Every stage applies rising-price decisions.

reviewChecklist.item: Scoring rewards decision quality rather than luck
reviewChecklist.notes: The investment outcome is separated from decision scoring.

reviewChecklist.item: Enjoyable spending is not automatically irresponsible
reviewChecklist.notes: Balanced entertainment remains valid.
The mixed path does not automatically receive the highest score.
The quiz tests purchasing power, budgeting, and affordability.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed within the specified duration
reviewChecklist.notes: Four compact stages, checkpoint, dashboard, and quiz fit eight minutes.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: Uses beginner-friendly adult language.
Every interaction includes non-gesture controls.

reviewChecklist.item: Final dashboard matches the simulation outcomes
reviewChecklist.notes: Results use tracked state sources.
Both outputs are generated from the same mission data.
